toc.title: Your state gets challenged throughout life

sections.title: Anchoring doesn't mean getting rid of defense
Don't try to get out of your defensive state
The want may be an impulse

blocks.p: Why do you have resistance to climbing your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) and accessing your safety state? Why does being in a defensive state seem like it's what your body wants?
One listener, a fellow therapist, sent me an email about exactly this. I'm going to break it into three parts, because each part raises its own question.

blocks.h: Your state gets challenged throughout life

blocks.p: The first part of the email:

q: In my own personal work, a question has come up for me. As background, I've got some childhood trauma and lived much of my life down the ladder, either in fight or flight or more in shutdown. A little before grad school and through grad school, I did a lot of my own work and feel like I moved into feeling more consistently in a safe and social state, rather than primarily in one of the lower two. However, after recently having a third child and dealing with lots of stressors, I've entered into a pretty depressive place.

blocks.p: Our polyvagal state gets challenged throughout our life. Our state is very much context-dependent. It depends on the literal safety or danger of our immediate environment, but also on the more passive safety or danger cues in that environment.

Right now, as I record this, the heater is on in the house. It makes a low, dull sound that's always there in the background while it runs. While it's on, there's a little more sympathetic energy for me that underlies everything I do. And when it turns off and there's silence, I can feel the difference: a kind of ease.

Same thing with the range hood over the stove. When we cook, my wife turns it on, and it just becomes part of the background noise. It's still on while we're eating dinner and while we're cleaning up afterwards. We don't consciously notice it, but it's there, and my body really reacts to that constant dull noise. It puts me in a little bit of a flight/fight kind of flavor. When I turn it off, I notice a little more ease.

So our state is very much dependent on our immediate environment, even the passive cues. It also depends on the people in our lives. If we're around people who have a negative influence on us, or who are stuck in their own defensive state, that's going to rub off on us. And it depends on family, on culture, on larger social factors. All of these come into play. So having less access to your safety state is normal and okay, depending on the context you live in.

As we age and gain new responsibilities and maturity and connections in life, we meet new obstacles and challenges, and these affect our capacity to be in our safety state. That includes things that are not obviously dangerous: things that are supposed to be positive growth points. Getting married, having kids, getting a new job. Quitting the job you need to quit, divorcing the person you need to divorce, leaving that friendship. Even putting in healthier boundaries between you and whoever needs them.
These are growth points and successes. They're not obviously dangerous, but they can activate one of your defensive states.

For me, one of my growth points has been all the business stuff, trying to sell my courses. I hired a coach a while back to help me through what was coming up for me around money. Generally, we want money. It provides greater access to things and can provide a more comfortable lifestyle. But for a lot of us, money doesn't feel that way. I was raised in a family where we didn't have a lot of money, so thinking bigger, thinking in terms of making more money or accomplishing more, was, and kind of still is, a much bigger challenge for me. Even something like that can activate our defensive state and keep us from growing where we want to grow.
Having kids was beautiful and wonderful, and there was absolutely a challenge to my capacity to access my safety state.

With new challenges and milestones in life comes less access to our safety state, because we don't have a map for it yet. We haven't navigated it yet. Over time, as we grow through these challenges, the safety state can develop.

In my opinion, we should be challenging the capacity of our safety state throughout life. I don't think we should be waiting until things are comfortable, or until things are perfectly ready to take that next step. It's going to be challenging. The fact that it's challenging means you might be on the right path. If it's super comfortable and easy, I don't think you're going to grow from that. I don't know if "waiting until things are right" even exists. The fact that things are difficult, or at least feel difficult, is potentially a good sign, depending on what it is.

Growth necessarily brings a challenge to our anchoring in safety. Challenge builds the strength of the safety pathways. It builds our capacity to handle stress while staying anchored in our safety state.

Defensive activation comes, and that's okay, because it's new. It's different. Having a third child, getting a new job, breaking up with someone who needs to be broken up with: there's going to be defensive state activation that comes with that. So can we stay anchored in safety while doing it? That's what helps exercise and build the strength of our vagal brake.
The second part of the email:

q: As my own therapist and I were looking at my depression in light of polyvagal theory, she was brainstorming ways to bring me back up the ladder, thinking through things I could do to re-regulate. However, I noticed lots of resistance to this. I was recognizing in myself a desire to stay in that shutdown space. We tried exploring what makes me want to stay there, but overall, I'm not really sure. I was wondering if you had insight into this.

blocks.p: When we have resistance to climbing the polyvagal ladder, there might be an impulse from our defensive state that we haven't met yet. I'll come back to impulses. First, I want to talk about acceptance, because accepting shutdown or accepting defensive state activation is different from trying to get out of it.

If you're in a defensive state, that is okay. It's not necessarily a bad thing. Even if it's a dysregulated defensive state, it's not bad. It is what it is. Ideally, we want to be anchored enough in safety that our stuck state can be present, or we can have some defensive activation, and we can tolerate it.

These states are not good or bad by themselves. They simply evolved within us to help us survive. There's no good or bad valuation to them. They might feel more good or more bad, sure. But you do have the state you're in. That's simply true. And you might be able to experience it, if you have enough of your safety state active at the same time.

You could also have more of a "fuck it" attitude, and that might be fine too. The way I look at it, it's happening anyway. If you can't get yourself out of it, okay, well, fuck it. It is what it is. I'm in my defensive state.

This comes up in therapy, where a person is in a defensive state, they're acknowledging it, and they say, "I can't do anything about it. I'm trying to anchor myself in safety. I'm trying to climb my polyvagal ladder. I'm trying to cope or ground myself or self-regulate," and it just persists. At that point, to me it's like, "Okay, fuck it, it is what it is. We'd better get some radical acceptance of this right now," and that might actually help us get to the next step.

I don't mean "fuck it" like destroy everything. It's more like, "Fuck it, I got this. I can do it. It's happening anyway. I might as well embrace it and get to the next step." There might actually be a little more fight energy in there, but it's not an out-of-control kind of "fuck it." It's that the state is present anyway, so there's no point in fighting it.

I don't want people fighting their polyvagal state. I don't think that helps. I think it's probably going to keep you down your ladder more than anything. So it's not about fighting the state. It's about noticing it and accepting it. That's validating that it's there: you do have these feelings, you do have these thoughts, whatever it is. That's the first step. And then, eventually, becoming curious about it and actually experiencing it.

blocks.h3: Anchoring doesn't mean getting rid of defense

blocks.p: Anchoring in safety, or climbing the polyvagal ladder, does not mean we need to ignore or work against the defensive state we're in. Quite the opposite.

When I'm working with clients in therapy, I try to get them to mindfully notice that they have a stuck defensive state, or some activation in that moment, and that that's okay. Can we allow it to be there? If we're ready, can we even invite it to be there? If it's there, can we allow it and treat it with respect? And can we also anchor ourselves in safety?
It's not about getting rid of the defensive state. It's not about fighting it, ignoring it, or minimizing it. It's allowing it to be there while also anchoring in safety.

Anchoring in safety does not mean you have no defensive state activation. Even climbing to the top of your polyvagal ladder doesn't necessarily mean you have no defensive state activation. It just means you're anchored in safety, so whatever defensive activation you have is not out of control. Being anchored is more about being regulated versus dysregulated. Dysregulated fight would be actually fighting somebody. Regulated fight energy would be experienced as power and motivation. So when you're anchored in safety, there might be some defensive state activation there, and that's okay. It might even be necessary, based on what's going on and where you're at in your trauma recovery.

blocks.h3: Don't try to get out of your defensive state

blocks.p: What I'd recommend to you is that you don't try to get out of your defensive state. I know that's kind of the opposite of what we hear about trauma recovery and polyvagal states, that the goal is somehow to get out of the defensive state. That's not the goal. You're in a defensive state for a reason, and you might be stuck in it for a reason. Fighting against that seems almost disrespectful to yourself.
Here's the process instead:

ol: Accept it. It is what it is.
Validate and normalize it. "I feel this way for a reason," a valid reason, a true reason. It's not made up. Validating and normalizing it might help you accept it.
Return your awareness to the defensive state. If you can anchor in safety, bring your attention back to the defensive state, this time from a mindfully curious, anchored, regulated state.
Listen to the sensations and impulses underneath the emotion of whatever defensive state you're in.

blocks.p: This is where we come back to impulses. If you act mindfully on the impulse that may be underneath the emotions you're going through, it will probably allow some ladder climbing to happen.

That process is a hell of a lot different from feeling some depressive shutdown stuff and saying, "I don't like this. What's wrong with me? I'd better climb my way out of this and up my polyvagal ladder." If you can do that, cool, go ahead. But I don't think it's that simple. I think there needs to be some "Hey, this is just where I'm at. This is simply what I feel, and that's okay. It is what it is."

You don't have to like it. It's not about that. It's about accepting: this is where I'm at, this is how I feel, and I probably feel this way for a reason. But to be able to do all of this, you do have to be anchored in your safety state first.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: The listener wrapped up her email:

q: I do feel like I want to stay in shutdown, particularly when I am there. When I'm not in the shutdown place, I see the benefit of moving into safety. But when I am shut down, I kind of want to be left alone to just be alone and stay in my misery.

blocks.p: I think a lot of people can echo this. So what does it mean to want to stay in shutdown?

You probably don't want to. If I asked you, "Do you want to exist in shutdown for the rest of your life?" you'd say, "No, I don't." But when you're in that state, it might feel like a want. So let's reframe what that want is.

blocks.h3: The want may be an impulse

blocks.p: Wanting might indicate that the body has a natural pull toward some of the impulses of shutdown, and then toward coming out when it's ready. The want might mean you're in shutdown and your body has some shutdown impulses it needs to complete. Then it'll come out and climb the polyvagal ladder when it's ready, and with shutdown that will be a slower process.

Wanting to be left alone, which she named, is very much a shutdown thing. In flight and fight you can also need space and want to be alone, but there's a different feel to it. With flight and fight there's more energy to it, more aggression or anxiety. In shutdown, it's an empty, heavy wanting to be left alone, isolating. It's just an emptiness.

It could also be wanting to be in situations of lower stimulation. If you're in a shutdown state, you're probably not going to have an impulse to go to a concert, or go up in a hot air balloon. You're probably not going to get into a race car and do some laps. I think you need some flight/fight energy for that. From a shutdown state, you'd probably have an impulse to be immobile or still, or to exist at a slower pace.

The goal with these impulses of your defensive state is to listen to them without judgment, and that's not easy. These impulses are tucked underneath our thoughts and our emotions, and even underneath the sensations we can consciously attune to. They're potentially buried pretty deep. To listen to them without judging them, you have to be anchored in your safety state.
To take the reframe further: rather than saying "I want," maybe it's "my body needs."

That means coming from a perspective of witnessing, a third-person observation of what your body needs. You and your body are one and the same, so this is a kind of splitting, which I'm not excited about, but conceptually it makes sense. It's not full-on curiosity and delving into your state. It's taking a step back and noticing what's actually happening: I do feel this way. I do have this impulse to be alone. I do have this impulse to be in lower stimulation. Maybe that means darkness.

If you can do that, if you can witness it, then once you're anchored in safety you can go to the direct experience and feel what that want is. You can feel the impulse within you. From your defensive state, what is the impulse? What's the action your body needs to go through? Or maybe it's the context: changing the environment you're in. For shutdown in particular, you'd probably do better with lower stimulation.
